tracks.title: The most abused word in software
tracks.text: Lesson three point five — trust. A sub-lesson, under toolkit. The most abused word in software. The parent page promised every toolkit is sandboxed, signed, shareable… and said the signature tells you who shipped it. Fair. But you've heard it before. [curious] npm has signatures. App stores have signatures. Package registries have signatures. And supply-chain attacks happen anyway… constantly… on signed ecosystems. So the honest question is not — is it signed. That word has been drained of meaning. The question is sharper. Two parts. First… what does the signature actually bind? Second… what concretely refuses to run when it fails? This whole lesson is the difference between a signature that proves someone with an account uploaded these bytes… and one that proves this exact set of promises was made by this exact author, and the build aborts the instant a byte of those promises changes. One stops almost nothing. The other stops a real attack.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Trust, for a toolkit, is an Ed25519 did:key signature over the canonical manifest body. It binds the declared contract — EXEC… CAPS… BUILD_SRC — to a self-certifying author identity. It is enforced by a build gate that refuses any unsigned or tampered third-party toolkit… and backed by the sandbox that bounds what runs regardless. [curious] Read that twice, because the surprising word is manifest… not code. The signature does not wrap the compiled bytes. It wraps the document where the toolkit states what it does. Everything else falls out of that one choice.

tracks.title: Two layers, distinct jobs
tracks.text: Two layers, distinct jobs. The parent gave the compressed version — the signature tells you who shipped it, and the sandbox bounds what it can do regardless of who shipped it. Unfold that into two layers that answer two different questions and defeat two different threats. Picture them side by side. Layer one is provenance — the signature. The question it answers… who promised exactly what? What defeats it… an author who mislabels their own toolkit, or code you imported knowingly. And what catches that… the sandbox, layer two, which bounds it regardless of the label. Layer two is the sandbox — capabilities plus isolation. The question it answers… what can happen, no matter who? What defeats it… nothing about identity, because it never asks who, only what. And what catches that gap… provenance, layer one, which tells you who to blame and detects tampering. [excited] That is the thesis. Provenance is identity-aware and tamper-detecting, but it cannot stop a malicious author who honestly signs malicious code. The sandbox is identity-blind, but it bounds a stranger's toolkit and a saint's toolkit identically. Stack them, and the gap in each is covered by the other. The mistake every we're-signed-you're-safe pitch makes… is shipping layer one and implying it does layer two's job. It can't.

tracks.title: An identity that carries its own proof
tracks.text: An identity that carries its own proof. Before the signature… the identity. In most signing systems the identity is a name that points at a key. You look up acme-corp in a registry, a server hands you their public key, and you trust the lookup. That lookup is the attack surface — a compromised registry hands you the wrong key. Here there is no lookup… because the identity is the public key. [curious] Picture the construction as a short chain. Start with the Ed25519 public key — thirty-two raw bytes. Glue a multicodec prefix in front of it — the bytes oh-eee-dee, oh-one. Base58 encode the result, with the Bitcoin alphabet. Then prepend a multibase tag… the letter z. What you get — did colon key colon z-six-M-k and so on — is the key itself, encoded. The same construction Radicle uses, the same the W3C spec describes. Nothing was registered anywhere. Which makes verification almost shockingly small. To check a signature, the verifier decodes the public key straight back out of the DID string — peeling the prefix off the front — and runs one crypto call. Hear the actual code. verify_sig of did, message, and signature… calls crypto dot verify, eddsa, with the public key of the did. And pub_of_did, given a string starting did colon key colon z, decodes the base58, strips the two prefix bytes, and returns the thirty-two-byte key. That's the entire P-K-I. No certificate authority. No registry server. No account. No network call. The verifier needs nothing but the manifest in front of it. [excited] Anyone — including a browser with no server behind it — can re-implement verification in a few lines. did:key is self-certifying… the identifier and the key it certifies are the same object.

tracks.title: What the signature actually binds
tracks.text: What the signature actually binds. Now the first aha. The signed bytes are the whole manifest body… and the manifest body is the declared contract. It's where the toolkit states, in plain keywords, everything a consumer would audit before trusting it. The source comment is blunt — the signature binds the declared contract to an author identity, so tampering with a vetted third-party toolkit is detectable. Picture a real manifest, with a bracket drawn around the signed region. Inside the bracket… the title. EXEC — what it runs. TRUST — its declared posture. CLI_BIN — the name it claims on the path. BUILD_LANG, and BUILD_SRC path-colon-src — where its bytes come from. ARG_MODE. An empty CAPS line — it claims no capabilities. And AUTHOR_DID — the identity, inside the signed bytes. Then the bracket closes… and the one line left outside is SIGNATURE. [curious] Notice the empty CAPS line is also inside the bracket. That is the whole scheme made concrete. An attacker's most valuable edit — quietly adding net-fetch to a toolkit that declared no network access — is exactly the byte change the signature catches. The thing worth protecting was never the binary. It's the claim… because the claim is what the consumer audited. And the binding is transitive. When BUILD_SRC points at a prebuilt artifact, the SHA256 pin sits inside the signed manifest too. The comment calls it plainly — the sha pin is the supply-chain gate… a compromised mirror cannot swap the binary. An unpinned fetch doesn't fail silently either — it prints a warning telling you to add the hash. So the signature reaches past the manifest… to the exact bytes the manifest fetches.

tracks.title: Strip-then-sign
tracks.text: Strip-then-sign — a depth rung, skippable, but it closes a real attack. There's a chicken-and-egg problem in signing a file that must contain its own signature — the moment you append the signature line, you've changed the bytes you just signed. The answer is a small canonicalization dance. Walk it as a conversation between two sides. On the author's side — the sign command — read the manifest body… strip any existing signature and author lines first… that's what makes re-signing idempotent, so signing twice yields a clean result instead of stacking lines. Then append a fresh AUTHOR_DID, trim, and sign that exact string. Write the body back, plus the signature line. On the consumer's side — the provenance check — read the manifest, strip only the signature line, trim… and you get byte-for-byte the same canonical body the author signed. Verify. You get an ok with the did… or a named failure. [curious] Here's the load-bearing detail. The AUTHOR_DID line is inside the signed bytes. Why that matters — imagine an attacker who wants to claim a vetted toolkit as their own. They swap the author DID to theirs. But now the signed body has changed, so the original signature no longer verifies… and they can't produce a new one without the original author's private key. The DID can't be swapped without re-signing the whole manifest, and re-signing needs a key they don't have. [excited] The identity is welded to the contract… not stapled beside it.

tracks.title: The gate that says refused
tracks.text: The gate that says refused. A signature nobody enforces is decoration. This one has teeth at three points in a toolkit's life — and the strongest stops a bad toolkit before a single byte compiles. Picture a manifest flowing into a decision. The question — what does TRUST say? If it's first-party, or absent, which defaults to first-party… it takes the left path and builds, no signature checked. If it's third-party, it takes the right — and provenance must verify. Three enforcement points. First… verify. The verify command appends one line to its report — a check-mark, third-party signature valid, with the did… or a cross, third-party provenance, the reason, and a nudge to sign. First-party toolkits get no such line. This is advisory — it tells you, but doesn't stop you. Second… build. The hard gate. A third-party toolkit whose provenance doesn't verify is refused with an exact string — the id, then REFUSED, third-party toolkit with invalid provenance, the reason, author must sign. The comment — an unsigned or tampered third-party toolkit never builds. The bytes never compile. Third… run. Even after a clean build, posture follows the toolkit into execution. A third-party command escalates one isolation rung… to node — a separate BEAM virtual machine — instead of the normal local subprocess. [curious] If distribution can't come up, it falls back gracefully to local — fail-open on availability, never on the work. A stranger's toolkit runs one wall further out, by default.

tracks.title: Reading a failure
tracks.text: Reading a failure — a depth rung. When a build prints REFUSED with a reason in parentheses, that reason is one of four atoms, checked in order. First… no_author_did — there's no author line, the manifest was never signed at all. The fix — sign it. Second… no_signature — an author DID is present but no signature line. The fix — sign it. Third… bad_signature_encoding — the signature line isn't valid Base64, corrupted or hand-edited. The fix — re-sign to overwrite it cleanly. Fourth… bad_signature — it decodes fine, but doesn't verify against the body, meaning the manifest was changed after signing. The fix — re-sign… and ask who changed which line. The verdict — the first two mean never signed, and you just sign. [curious] The fourth is the one that matters. It means the bytes and the signature disagree — precisely the tamper case the scheme exists to catch. If you see it on a toolkit you didn't change, the manifest changed under you… and the next question isn't how do I make this build. It's what got edited. Hear the whole round trip. You run sign on huniq — it returns, signed huniq as did colon key colon z-six-M-k and so on. An attacker edits one line — flipping an empty CAPS to CAPS net-fetch. You run build. And back comes — huniq, REFUSED, third-party toolkit with invalid provenance, bad_signature, author must sign huniq. [excited] The edit could have been any manifest byte. EXEC, BUILD_SRC, the SHA256 pin, even the author DID itself. Every one lands at bad_signature… and every one is refused before compilation.

tracks.title: One key, three rails
tracks.text: One key, three rails — a depth rung. The same tenant did:key isn't just a toolkit thing. It signs three surfaces across the ecosystem from one keypair, with three verify points. Picture one keypair at the top, fanning into three rails. Rail one… toolkit manifests, signed by the sign-text function, verified at the build gate. Rail two… published workbook HTML — an embedded c2pa-style manifest, plus an asset hash of the file itself. Rail three… agent run ledgers, the attributable signed half of the record. [curious] The middle rail is the one a consumer meets at install time. A published workbook carries an embedded manifest — an Ed25519 signature over canonical, key-sorted JSON, plus an asset-sha-256 of the file. At install, the library checks both — the signature, and that the artifact hasn't changed since. A tampered bundle fails with bad_signature. An unsigned one fails as unverifiable. A test proves it the honest way — append a comment after signing, and the integrity check catches it. On the command line, verify on a file is pure-read, no key needed, and prints valid, signature, asset-integrity, issuer. The deliberate part — the manifest module says it outright… no C2PA stack, no X.509, no Rust signer binary. The did:key supersedes the planned cert path. [excited] It is, roughly, C2PA's idea — provenance that travels with the bytes — without C2PA's certificate machinery. One small self-certifying key… three places it proves authorship… zero infrastructure to stand up.

tracks.title: Why your own toolkits skip this
tracks.text: Why your own toolkits skip this. The obvious objection — if signing is so important, why does a first-party toolkit skip every check? It's a deliberate threat-model decision, and the source is candid about the tension. The discovery root — the toolkits directory — is, in the comment's own words… an unauthenticated, writable directory. A toolkit dropped there is untrusted supply-chain input… not first-party by virtue of its location. So location does not confer trust. [curious] What confers it is something else. For your own in-tree toolkits, the repo's own review-and-commit process is the trust mechanism. The comment finishes the thought — location-trust is fine for our own repo. The signature exists for code that crossed an org boundary — a toolkit from a stranger, fetched from somewhere, that your review process never touched. For that, you need cryptographic provenance. For code that went through your pull requests… you already have a trust mechanism, and it's a better one than a signature — human review, with history. This is why promotion writes TRUST first-party. When you promote a toolkit you authored, it's yours… and trust is relative to who's running it. The same toolkit a third-party consumer installs would have them granting its capabilities at install time. [excited] Trust isn't a property baked into the toolkit. It's the relationship between the toolkit and the person running it.

tracks.title: The honest edges
tracks.text: The honest edges. This lesson owes some real limits — and stating them is the whole reason the thesis is two layers, not one. First… the trust label is self-declared. The TRUST keyword lives in the manifest the author controls. The gate detects tampering with a vetted third-party toolkit — it does not detect mislabeling. A malicious author who writes first-party skips the signature check entirely. What saves you then isn't provenance — it's that you imported it knowingly, and the sandbox and granted caps still bound it. Layer two, doing its job. Second… the signature covers the manifest, not the prose. Skills, and path-colon source directories, aren't under the signature. What bounds them is the sha-pinned content-addressed artifact for prebuilts, the sandbox and granted caps at run time, and registration containment that rejects wasm outside the commands directory. Third… there's no signed third-party catalog yet. Honestly — no in-tree toolkit currently carries a signature. All of them are first-party, by design. The third-party gate is exercised by tests and the install rail… not yet by a public signed catalog. The mechanism is real and tested. The ecosystem around it is young. Fourth… isolation fails open. The run-time escalation to a separate node falls back to the local subprocess if distribution can't start. A deliberate availability choice — but it means the extra wall is best-effort, not a guarantee. [curious] Every edge points at the same conclusion. The signature is a sharp tool for one job — who promised exactly what, and has it been changed — and a useless tool for the other — what can this code actually do to me. That second job belongs to the sandbox… explicit capability grants… reserved built-in names that can never be shadowed… and the sha pins. Provenance and sandbox. Distinct jobs. Layered. Neither pretending to be the other.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I need to sign my own first-party toolkits? No — and not because we got lazy. Your repo's review-and-commit process is the trust mechanism for code you authored, and it's stronger than a signature. The signature is for code that crossed an org boundary. What if I lose my signing key? A fresh keypair mints a fresh DID — a new identity, with no claim on anything the old one signed. That's why the signing-key seed exists — held as a deploy secret, it restores the same keypair, and the same DID, across redeploys. Can someone re-sign my toolkit as theirs? Yes — and that's honest. They can strip your signature and sign with their key. What they cannot do is keep your signature while claiming authorship, because your DID is inside the signed bytes. [chuckles] The signature proves who shipped this exact contract… not copyright. Is this C2PA? It's C2PA's idea without C2PA's machinery. Provenance that travels with the bytes — yes. Cert chains, X.509, a Rust signer binary — deliberately no. What breaks the signature? Any byte of the manifest body. And — if it can't stop a malicious author, what's the point? Different job. The signature stops silent tampering with a toolkit you already vetted. It does not stop a known-bad author shipping known-bad code — the sandbox does that. [excited] Two layers, distinct jobs. Install neither alone.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's trust. The signature binds the promise — the declared contract, not the code. Change a promise after the author signed, and the build is refused before a byte compiles. The identity carries its own proof — did:key is the public key, verification needs no registry, no CA, no account. And still… provenance tells you who promised what. The sandbox bounds what happens regardless. Neither replaces the other. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under toolkit — the parent page that holds both layers, floor, manual, and muscle. Next door sits verification, the quality gate this signature is one line of… and sandboxes, layer two, the part that bounds the rest. Read the parent next. The cheque it wrote… is now cashed.
